title: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
hookLine: the Ansar chief whose death shook the Throne (Bukhari)

lines: NOT A PROPHET, NOT A KING.
cards: The Throne of the Most Merciful shook. That's the sentence. Jabir ibn Abdullah says he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say it, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it, in a chapter about one man.
Not a prophet. Not a king. The chief of a clan in Medina, wounded in battle, who died of the wound.
What kind of life gets a sentence like that at its end? Today: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.

teach.b: Sa'd was a leader of the Aws, a tribe of Medina, and the early biographies say that when he accepted Islam, his clan followed him. He was a chief, with people looking at him. Bukhari shows what that looked like.
Sa'd went to Mecca to perform the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, staying with an old friend there.

teach.h: FACING ABU JAHL AT THE KAABA.
teach.b: Abu Jahl, a leader of the Prophet's opponents, stopped him at the Kaaba and sneered that he was walking around safely after giving shelter to the Prophet's people. Sa'd didn't lower his voice.
If you stop me from this, he said, I'll stop you from something worse: your trade road to Syria, which runs past Medina. A chief speaking as a chief, for the people under his protection.
At the battle of the Trench, Sa'd was hit by an arrow in the arm; we met the tent where he was cared for, Rufaydah's tent in the mosque.

In his last days he was also asked to give a judgment in a hard and painful case, one the histories record and readers still wrestle with; that story needs its own day. The wound did not heal, and he died of it.
That's when the Prophet said the Throne shook. Bukhari adds another scene. Someone gave the Prophet a garment of silk, and people kept touching it, amazed at how soft it was.
The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise, the Prophet said, are better than this.

A small, everyday thing, finer than the softest thing in the room. Sa'd held one role, chief of his people, and held it the same way in Mecca, in battle, and in a tent with a wound that wouldn't close.

how: Muslims remember Sa'd ibn Mu'adh from reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, above all the Prophet's words that the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at his death.

o: the Meccan leader who stopped pilgrims at the Kaaba
the governor Umar sent to rule over Syria
the chief of Medina at whose death the Throne shook

games.q: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh — tap the pairs.

s: Sa'd backed down when Abu Jahl threatened him in Mecca
he threatened to cut off Mecca's trade road to Syria.
the Prophet compared Sa'd's handkerchiefs in Paradise to a silk garment
they are better than this, he said, in Bukhari.
Sa'd recovered fully from his wound at the Trench
the wound did not heal, and he died of it.

games.q: you are Sa'd, at the Kaaba in Mecca. Abu Jahl sneers that you walk safely after sheltering the Prophet's people. what do you do?
o: answer: stop me, and I'll stop your trade road to Syria.
games.why: Bukhari keeps his answer: block me from this, and I'll block something worse for you, your road to Syria.

practice: You hold more than one role: parent, child, friend, worker, neighbor. Choose one and ask where, in it, you are one person in public and another in private, then let one small difference close; not all of them, one.
If you pray, you can ask for sincerity, which Muslims call ikhlas, in that one role.

wordCard.voice: Sa'd. The chief of Medina who stood up to Abu Jahl, was wounded at the Trench, and at whose death, the Prophet said, the Throne shook. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Throne shook, the words the Prophet said at Sa'd's death.

carryVoice: Your line: the throne shook. One role, held the same way everywhere. Day eight hundred fifty-six, done.
